text: American Express Company, a globally integrated payments company founded in 1850 and incorporated in 1965 as a New York corporation, operates as a bank holding company under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, and is subject to supervision and examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The company provides credit and charge cards to consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations worldwide through its various products and services, available via mobile and online applications, affiliate marketing, customer referral programs, third-party service providers, direct mail, telephone, in-house sales teams, and direct response advertising. Its businesses are organized into four reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS), with corporate functions and certain other businesses included in Corporate & Other. The company’s end-to-end integrated payments platform connects Card Members and merchants through direct relationships, enabling access to spending data for risk underwriting, fraud reduction, and targeted marketing, while protecting data in compliance with applicable policies and laws. It also obtains data through contractual relationships with third-party card issuers, merchant acquirers, aggregators, and processors. The company’s global proprietary card-issuing businesses are conducted through USCS, CS, and ICS, offering a broad range of card products, rewards, and services to consumers and commercial customers, with a focus on attracting Millennial and Gen Z customers and expanding SME offerings through products like business checking and consumer rewards checking, as well as digital capabilities from acquisitions of Kabbage, Resy, and acompay. The ICS organization consolidates consumer, SME, and large commercial card issuing activities outside the U.S. to better serve local priorities, with significant billed business in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, Japan, Canada, and Mexico. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide billed business (spending on American Express cards issued by the company) was $1,338 billion, and the company had 76.7 million proprietary cards-in-force worldwide. The GMNS segment manages relationships with millions of merchants globally, including signing new merchants, setting discount rates, and handling merchant servicing, and operates through programs like OptBlue® that allow third-party acquirers to contract directly with small merchants. The company also provides fraud-prevention tools, marketing solutions, and data analytics to merchants and partners. Through its card network, American Express operates in approximately 103 countries and territories, licensing the American Express brand to third-party banks and institutions to issue local currency cards and serve as merchant acquirers. For the year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide network services processed volume (spending on American Express cards issued by third parties) was $214.5 billion, and the company had 56.5 million cards-in-force issued by third parties worldwide. The company’s diverse customer base includes consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations, with a global footprint supported by partnerships. Key partners include Delta Air Lines, Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide Holdings, British Airways, Amazon.com (via Pay with Points), PayPal, i2c, BILL, BillTrust, Versapay, and Fine Hotels and Resorts. Delta is the company’s largest strategic partner, with the Delta cobrand portfolio representing approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. The Delta cobrand portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards, with the current agreement running through the end of 2029 and the company planning significant investments in the partnership. Delta also participates in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits such as airport lounge access, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and serves as a corporate payments customer. The company’s spend-centric business model generates revenue primarily by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate market value of the registrant’s voting shares held by non-affiliates was approximately $104.0 billion based on the closing sale price on the New York Stock Exchange. As of February 2, 2023, there were 744,192,702 common shares outstanding. The company is a well-known seasoned issuer and has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has submitted electronically every Interactive Data File required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T and is classified as a large accelerated filer. Revenues and expenses related to Delta are significant and represent a major source of value for American Express Card Members. The Delta cobrand portfolio accounted for approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. This portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards. The current Delta cobrand agreement extends through the end of 2029, and the company expects to continue making significant investments in this partnership. Delta is also a key participant in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits and services including airport lounge access for certain American Express Card Members, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and is a corporate payments customer. American Express works with all partners to deliver value, choice, and unique experiences to its customer base. The company’s “spend-centric” business model primarily generates revenue by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. Spending on American Express cards is, on average, higher per card than that of competitors, offering merchants loyal customers and larger transactions, which in turn enables the company to invest in attractive rewards, targeted marketing, and other programs for both Card Members and merchants. This model differentiates American Express cards and provides value to Card Members, merchants, and business partners. The American Express brand, known for trust, security, and service, is among the most valuable globally and is protected through extensive investment in trademarks, service marks, and patents worldwide. The company aims to deliver the world’s best customer experience daily, with its reputation for service recognized through numerous awards. Customer care professionals, travel consultants, and partners are trained to enhance the brand experience and deepen customer relationships. American Express focuses on four strategic imperatives: expanding leadership in the premium consumer space by offering benefits across everyday spending, borrowing, travel, and lifestyle needs, expanding global business partnerships, and creating experiences that attract high-spending customers; building on its strong position in commercial payments by evolving card value propositions, differentiating corporate card and accounts payable solutions, and introducing innovative financing, banking, and payment products for business customers; strengthening its global, integrated network by increasing merchant acceptance, providing fraud protection, marketing insights, and connections to high-spending Card Members, and collaborating with network partners to expand offerings; and leveraging its unique global position to support its other strategic goals. Previously, a strategic imperative to make American Express an essential part of customers’ digital lives has become embedded in the company’s operations. The company also has an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategy with three pillars: promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DE&I) to foster a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workforce and society; advancing climate solutions by enhancing operations to meet customer and community needs in a low-carbon future; and building financial confidence by offering responsible, secure, and transparent products and services to help individuals and businesses achieve financial resilience. The company emphasizes a culture built on supportive relationships and inclusivity, where colleagues feel welcome, heard, and supported in their growth. This culture is guided by the Blue Box Values: We Do What's Right, We Embrace Diversity, We Back Our Customers, We Stand for Equity and Inclusion, We Make It Great, We Win as a Team, We Respect People, and We Support Communities. As of December 31, 2022, American Express employed approximately 77,300 colleagues, with about 26,000 in the United States and 51,300 outside the United States. The company added colleagues in 2022 to support business growth. To attract and retain top talent, it offers competitive compensation and leading benefits and invests in programs such as on-the-job learning tools, cross-border assignments, career coaching, mentoring, rotation opportunities, virtual learning, and formal classroom instruction. The health and wellness of colleagues is a priority, with a holistic approach addressing physical, financial, and mental well-being. In 2022, the company launched Amex Flex, allowing colleagues to work in the office, at home, or in a hybrid model based on role and business needs, to broaden the talent pool and improve retention. An annual Colleague Experience Survey showed that 92 percent of participating colleagues would recommend American Express as a great place to work. The 2022 company scorecard included talent retention, colleague engagement, and diversity representation goals. As of December 31, 2022, women made up 53.7 percent of the global workforce, and in the U.S. workforce, Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic/Latinx colleagues represented 18.7 percent, 17.9 percent, and 14.2 percent, respectively, based on preliminary 2022 U.S. EEO-1 data. Fifty-two percent of the Executive Committee were women or from diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds (based on self-identified characteristics). The company regularly reviews compensation practices to ensure fairness across genders globally and across races and ethnicities in the U.S., considering factors such as role, level, tenure, performance, and geography. American Express competes globally in the payments industry with card networks, issuers, acquirers, paper-based transactions, bank transfers, and emerging alternative payment and financing mechanisms such as digital wallets, open banking, buy now, pay later products, real-time settlement systems, financial technology companies, digital currencies, blockchain, prepaid systems, and gift cards. As a card issuer, it competes with financial institutions offering general-purpose credit and debit cards, private label card issuers, mobile wallet providers, and companies offering credit. It faces intense competition in the premium segment and for cobrand relationships, as well as for partners and differentiated offerings like airport lounge access. The company competes with other global card networks, including China UnionPay, Visa, Mastercard, JCB, Discover, and Diners Club International (owned by Discover), and is the fourth largest general-purpose card network globally by purchase volume. Other companies, including merchant acquirers, processors, and digital platforms like Alipay, PayPal, and Venmo, as well as regional networks like the National Payments Corporation of India, perform similar activities. Key competitive factors include product and service features, brand reputation, customer spending and credit performance, merchant acceptance, value proposition attractiveness, availability of alternative payment and financing options, marketing effectiveness, innovation speed, expense management tools, and data capabilities, particularly for business customers, and the security of cardholder, merchant, and network partner information. The rapid growth of alternative payment mechanisms, including financial services integration and closed-loop loyalty features, presents ongoing competitive challenges. Additionally, the company faces significant government regulation and supervision worldwide, with substantial compliance costs, and regulatory scrutiny, high expectations, and unpredictable enforcement environments.

Results may materially suffer due to substantial and increasingly intense global competition in the payments industry, as discussed in the “Risk Factors” section, and the business is subject to comprehensive government regulation and supervision, which could materially adversely affect operations and financial condition. Legal proceedings related to provisions in merchant contracts—such as non-discrimination and honor-all-cards—could have a material adverse effect on the business, leading to additional litigation or arbitrations, changes to merchant agreements or business practices, substantial monetary damages, and reputational harm. The Company, TRS, and its U.S. bank subsidiary, American Express National Bank (AENB), are subject to extensive federal and state banking laws, regulations, and policies, including oversight by the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Both the Company and TRS are consolidatedly supervised by the Federal Reserve, with AENB under OCC supervision. The Company and TRS have elected financial holding company status, which allows broader financial activities, but must maintain eligibility requirements, including being “well capitalized” and “well managed,” and AENB receiving a “satisfactory” CRA rating. The Company and its subsidiaries are prohibited from engaging in practices deemed unsafe or unsound by regulators, who have discretion in determining safe and sound operations. Acquisitions and investments are subject to regulatory review and approval by the Federal Reserve and OCC, with broad discretion in evaluations. The Company is subject to U.S. federal bank regulatory rules that categorize bank holding companies based on risk indicators, placing the Company in Category IV. As a Category IV firm, it is not subject to advanced approaches capital requirements and must maintain minimum capital ratios of 4.5% CET1, 6.0% Tier 1, and 8.0% Total capital to risk-weighted assets. The Company is subject to a dynamic stress capital buffer (SCB) of 2.5% CET1 capital, effective from October 1 each year, increasing the effective minimum ratios to 7.0% CET1, 8.5% Tier 1, and 10.5% Total capital. AENB is subject to a static 2.5% capital conservation buffer. The Company must maintain a leverage ratio of at least 4.0%. Liquidity requirements under the Federal Reserve’s enhanced prudential standards include a liquidity buffer and a minimum liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), but Category IV firms with less than $50 billion in weighted short-term wholesale funding, like the Company, are not subject to specific LCR or net stable funding ratio (NSFR) requirements. The Company participates in supervisory stress testing every other year, with the most recent test in 2022, and must submit an annual capital plan by April 5. The SCB based on stress tests is recalculated every other year, and the firm may elect to participate in an “off year” to receive an updated SCB. Capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, are limited if capital ratios fall below minimums or if the capital plan is resubmitted. AENB’s ability to pay dividends to TRS is restricted by law and requires approval from the OCC if not paid from recent earnings or if it would breach capital adequacy. The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDIA) imposes progressive restrictions on institutions based on capital categories, with AENB required to maintain CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, and Tier 1 leverage ratios of at least 6.5%, 8.0%, 10.0%, and 5.0%, respectively, to be considered “well capitalized.” AENB may be prohibited from accepting brokered deposits or offering interest rates above prevailing market rates unless well capitalized or adequately capitalized with a waiver. The Company is not required to submit a holding company resolution plan, but AENB must submit a resolution plan every three years, with the most recent submission in December 2022. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important institution in the event of default and systemic risk, with significant differences from the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, including the FDIC’s authority to disregard creditor claim priorities.

AENB is required to prepare and submit a separate resolution plan to the FDIC to enable the FDIC, as receiver, to effectively resolve the institution under the FDIA in the event of failure. Under the FDIC’s rule and its June 2021 statement, insured depository institutions with $100 billion or more in assets—such as AENB—are required to submit resolution plans on a three-year cycle, and AENB submitted its most recent resolution plan in December 2022 as required. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important financial institution if the Company is in danger of default and poses a systemic risk to U.S. financial stability. Under the OLA, the FDIC has broad powers as receiver, including the ability to disregard the strict priority of creditor claims in limited circumstances, use an administrative claims procedure instead of judicial proceedings, and transfer claims to a “bridge” entity. The FDIC has developed a “single point of entry” (SPOE) strategy under OLA, whereby the FDIC would transfer AENB’s assets—including shares of its operating subsidiaries—and potentially limited liabilities to a “bridge” holding company; use the failed company’s resources to recapitalize its subsidiaries; and satisfy unsecured creditor claims and other claimants by delivering securities from new financial companies emerging from the bridge entity. Under this strategy, management of the failed holding company would be replaced, and shareholders and creditors would bear the losses. If the FDIC is appointed conservator or receiver of AENB, it has the power to transfer any of AENB’s assets or liabilities to a new obligor without creditor approval, enforce contractual terms, or repudiate or disaffirm contracts or leases deemed burdensome by the FDIC. Additionally, claims of U.S. deposit holders and certain administrative expenses of the FDIC would be prioritized over other general unsecured claims, including those of debt holders and depositors in non-U.S. offices, meaning such non-U.S. depositors could receive substantially less or nothing compared to U.S. office depositors. The Company is required to act as a source of financial and managerial strength to its U.S. bank subsidiary, AENB, and may be required to commit capital or financial resources to support AENB even when it would otherwise not do so. Capital loans to AENB are subordinate to deposits and certain other indebtedness of AENB, and in the event of the Company’s bankruptcy, any commitment to a federal banking regulator to maintain AENB’s capital would be assumed by the bankruptcy trustee and given priority of payment. Certain transactions between AENB and its affiliates—including the Company, TRS, and their subsidiaries—are subject to quantitative and qualitative limitations, collateral requirements, and other restrictions under statute and regulation and must generally be made on an arm’s-length basis. AENB accepts deposits insured by the FDIC up to applicable limits, and the FDIC may terminate such insurance if AENB engages in unsafe or unsound practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition, or violates applicable laws, regulations, rules, orders, or conditions. There is no known practice, condition, or violation at AENB that would lead to termination of deposit insurance. The FDIC’s deposit insurance fund is funded by assessments on insured institutions, including AENB, which are subject to adjustment by the FDIC. AENB is subject to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), which imposes affirmative, ongoing obligations to meet the credit needs of local communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. In May 2022, federal banking agencies issued a joint notice of proposed rulemaking proposing revisions to CRA regulations, including changes to assessment areas, evaluation frameworks, performance standards, definitions of community development activities, and data collection and reporting. The U.S. banking agencies have increased their focus on climate risk-related supervision; on December 16, 2021, the OCC issued for public comment proposed “Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management for Large Banks,” which apply to OCC-regulated institutions with over $100 billion in total consolidated assets, such as AENB, and cover governance, policies, strategic planning, risk management, data and reporting, and scenario analysis. The principles also offer guidance on incorporating climate risks into traditional risk categories. On March 30, 2022, and December 2, 2022, the FDIC and the Federal Reserve, respectively, issued for public comment similar draft principles for financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets under their supervision, including the Company. It is too early to determine what regulations or policies may be adopted or applied, and the potential impact on the Company and AENB remains uncertain. The Company’s consumer-oriented activities are regulated in the U.S. and internationally; in the U.S., the CFPB supervises and examines marketing, sale, and servicing of consumer financial products and enforces federal consumer financial laws, including preventing “unfair, deceptive, or abusive” practices, collecting fines, requiring restitution, engaging in consumer education, tracking complaints, requesting data, and promoting access to underserved consumers. U.S. state laws also impose significant consumer credit protection, disclosure, and other requirements, some of which are more stringent than federal laws. Federal law also regulates abusive debt collection practices, which can affect the Company’s ability to collect amounts owed and subject it to regulatory scrutiny. On February 1, 2023, the CFPB issued a proposed rule to lower the safe harbor amount for late fees considered “reasonable and proportional” to costs incurred by credit card issuers, eliminate annual inflation adjustments, and prohibit late fees above 25% of the consumer’s required minimum payment; if adopted, this rule is not expected to become effective before 2024. The Company is also subject to “money transmitter” or “sale of check” laws in most U.S. states, unclaimed and abandoned property laws requiring payment of face amounts of uncashed Travelers Cheques or unredeemed prepaid cards after a specified period, and insurance laws in the U.S. and other countries where it offers insurance services. Outside the U.S., regulators focus on consumer protection (e.g., EU, UK, Canada) and responsible lending (e.g., Australia, Mexico, New Zealand, Singapore), with increasing emphasis on customer outcomes rather than compliance. Regulators are placing greater emphasis on firms’ compliance, risk, and control frameworks, particularly in systems and controls for identifying and resolving issues. In various jurisdictions, legislators and regulators have focused on card network operations, including enforcement actions, legislation, and regulations affecting interchange fees, merchant card acceptance, and pricing, and establishing ongoing oversight of payment systems. Regulation of interchange fees has negatively impacted and may continue to negatively impact the Company’s discount revenue due to downward pressure on merchant discount rates from reduced competitor pricing under interchange fee caps. The Company has exited its network businesses in the EU and Australia due to regulation in those jurisdictions. There is uncertainty regarding when or how interchange fee caps and other provisions of EU payments legislation might apply in cobrand partnerships and agent arrangements in the EU, and differing regulatory interpretations could lead to regulatory action, penalties, or the loss of existing cobrand and agent relationships. In certain EU Member States and Australia, merchants are permitted by law to surcharge card purchases. In the U.S., laws prohibiting surcharging have been overturned, and some states have passed or are considering surcharging laws. Effective October 6, 2022, merchants in Canada (excluding Quebec) are permitted to surcharge credit card purchases up to a maximum of 2.4%, resulting from a litigation settlement with Visa and Mastercard. Surcharging is an adverse customer experience and could materially harm the Company, especially if it disproportionately affects credit card usage or card usage generally, its Card Members, or its business. Other steering or differential acceptance practices permitted by regulation in some jurisdictions could also have a material adverse effect. In some countries, governments require international card networks to be locally licensed or to localize operations; for example, India’s Reserve Bank of India, under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, mandated local storage of payment data and imposed restrictions on American Express Banking Corp. in 2021, which were lifted in August 2022 after significant investment in technology, infrastructure, and resources to comply. The development and enforcement of such laws may adversely affect the Company’s ability to compete and maintain its global network. Regulatory and legislative activity in privacy, data protection, data governance, information, and cyber security continues to increase worldwide. The Company has established and maintains policies and a governance framework to comply with applicable laws and meet evolving customer and industry expectations. Regulators are increasingly focused on ensuring that privacy, data protection, cyber security policies and practices adequately inform customers about data collection, use, sharing, and security, provide them with choices, and appropriately safeguard personal information and account access. Regulators also emphasize data management, resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management. In the U.S., certain businesses are subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) and its regulations, which limit sharing of consumers’ nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties and require a written comprehensive information security program appropriate to the business size, complexity, and sensitivity of customer data. The Company has expanded privacy rights for California residents under the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020. Various U.S. regulators, states, and territories are considering or have adopted privacy or cyber security laws that may be more stringent or expansive than federal requirements. The Company is also subject to privacy, data protection, data governance, and cyber security laws in other countries, including the EU, Australia, Canada, China, Japan, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Singapore, Thailand, and the UK, some of which are more stringent or expansive than U.S. laws and may conflict with each other. Some jurisdictions impose onerous requirements for transferring personal data to other jurisdictions, while others require in-country data processing or storage. Compliance increases technology, administrative, and other costs, limits the ability to optimize closed-loop data, and may require local technology services. Some laws also require broader access to data and intellectual property by foreign governments or third parties. Data breach and operational outage notification laws, as well as regulatory activities promoting such notifications and resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management, are becoming more prevalent in jurisdictions outside the U.S. In Europe, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) imposes legal and compliance obligations on companies processing personal data of individuals in the EU, regardless of location, with potential fines up to 4% of total worldwide annual revenue. The GDPR requires prompt notification of data breaches to affected individuals and supervisory authorities. The UK GDPR mirrors the GDPR’s compliance requirements and fine structure. In October 2022, an Executive Order, together with U.S. Department of Justice regulations, was signed to implement a new data privacy framework for cross-border transfers of EU personal data to the U.S. The Company is also subject to significant supervision and an increasingly stringent enforcement environment regarding compliance with anti-money laundering (AML), countering the financing of terrorism (CFT), economic sanctions, and anti-corruption laws. Failure to maintain adequate AML/CFT, sanctions, and anti-corruption programs and procedures could result in material financial, legal, and reputational consequences. In the U.S., AML/CFT requirements primarily stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Bank Secrecy Act), as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws, with many statutory provisions requiring additional rulemakings, reports, and measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements are largely derived from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws.

We are subject to a significant number of anti-money laundering and counterfinancing of terrorism (AML/CFT) laws and regulations globally. In the United States, the majority of AML/CFT requirements stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and the regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, collectively known as the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws. Many of its statutory provisions will require additional rulemakings, reports, and other measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements arise primarily from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws and regulations. Numerous other countries, including Argentina, Australia, Canada, India, Mexico, New Zealand, and Russia, have enacted or proposed new or enhanced AML/CFT legislation applicable to American Express. These laws and regulations require us to establish AML/CFT programs that meet certain standards, including expanded reporting—particularly on suspicious transactions—and enhanced information gathering and recordkeeping. Our AML/CFT programs have faced heightened scrutiny in some countries, including certain EU Member States. Any errors, failures, or delays in complying with AML/CFT laws, perceived deficiencies in our programs, or an association of our business with money laundering, terrorist financing, tax fraud, or other illicit activity can lead to significant supervisory, criminal, and civil proceedings and lawsuits, resulting in substantial penalties, forfeiture of assets, loss of licenses, restrictions on business activities, or other enforcement actions. We are also subject to economic sanctions imposed by national governments and international bodies such as the United Nations and the EU, targeting individuals, entities, vessels, governments, and countries that threaten their interests or violate international norms. These sanctions are used to advance foreign policy goals such as conflict resolution, counterterrorism, counternarcotics, and promotion of democracy and human rights. Failure to comply can result in serious legal and reputational consequences, including criminal penalties. The United States has imposed sanctions affecting transactions with designated foreign countries, nationals, and others, prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging with individuals or entities listed as “Specially Designated Nationals” (such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers) without a license or authorization. These prohibitions are administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which prohibits financial transactions with such entities, requires the blocking of assets in which they have an interest, and bans transfers of property subject to U.S. jurisdiction. Blocked assets, such as property or bank deposits, cannot be paid out, withdrawn, set off, or transferred without an OFAC license. We maintain a global sanctions compliance program to meet the requirements of applicable sanctions regimes. We are also subject to complex anti-corruption laws, including the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the UK Bribery Act, and other laws that prohibit improper payments. The FCPA makes it illegal to offer or provide anything of value to foreign government officials, political parties, or political party officials to obtain or retain business or an improper advantage. It also requires strict compliance with accounting and internal controls. The UK Bribery Act prohibits commercial bribery and receipt of bribes and makes it a corporate offense to fail to prevent bribery by an associated person, in addition to prohibiting improper payments to foreign government officials. Failure by us or our colleagues, contractors, or agents to comply with the FCPA, the UK Bribery Act, or similar laws can result in investigations, prosecutions, and potentially severe criminal and civil penalties. Our compensation practices are overseen by the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Federal banking regulators’ guidance on sound incentive compensation practices outlines three key principles: (1) incentives should appropriately balance risk and financial results without encouraging imprudent risk-taking, (2) incentive plans must be compatible with effective internal controls and risk management, and (3) they must be supported by strong corporate governance, including active and effective oversight by the board of directors. Deficiencies in our compensation practices identified by regulators may be incorporated into our supervisory ratings, affecting our ability to make acquisitions or perform other actions. Enforcement actions may be taken if our incentive compensation arrangements or related risk-management or governance processes are found to pose a risk to our safety and soundness and we have not taken prompt and effective corrective measures. The Dodd-Frank Act requires U.S. financial regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the SEC, to adopt rules on incentive-based payment arrangements for entities with at least $1 billion in total assets. In 2016, the federal banking regulators, the SEC, the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration proposed revised rules on incentive-based compensation practices, which have not yet been finalized. If adopted in a form similar to the proposal, these rules would impose limitations on how we structure compensation for our colleagues, potentially harming our ability to hire, retain, and motivate key personnel. In October 2022, the SEC adopted a new rule requiring national securities exchanges to mandate policies that require the recovery of excess incentive-based compensation paid to current or former executive officers in the case of a restatement of previously issued financial statements, and require listed issuers to disclose any recovery analysis triggered by such restatements. The company uses an Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM) program to identify, aggregate, monitor, measure, report, and manage risks, defining risk appetite, governance, culture, and capabilities, with the Chief Risk Officer leading its implementation. Risk management is overseen by the Board of Directors through three committees: the Risk Committee, the Audit and Compliance Committee, and the Compensation and Benefits Committee, each composed entirely of independent directors and meeting regularly with senior management. The Risk Committee oversees the ERM framework, approves the ERM policy, and reviews risk appetite across credit, operational, compliance, reputational, market, funding, liquidity, model, strategic, business, country, and environmental, social, and governance risks, including limits and escalation triggers. It reviews the appointment, performance, and compensation of the Chief Risk Officer and monitors risk profile against tolerances, compliance with regulatory capital and liquidity standards, and CCAR submissions. The Audit and Compliance Committee reviews compliance policies, including the Compliance Risk Tolerance Statement, the effectiveness of the Corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, financial statement integrity, internal and external auditing, and internal audit performance and independence. It approves the Chief Audit Executive’s appointment, performance, and compensation, and reviews the annual audit plan, charter, policies, budget, staffing, and risk assessment methodology. The Compensation and Benefits Committee works with the Chief Risk Officer to balance risk with business incentives, sets risk goals, reviews business unit risk profiles, and uses a risk-balanced incentive framework to determine bonus pools and senior executive compensation. The Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC), chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is the highest-level management committee overseeing firm-wide risks, maintaining the enterprise-wide risk appetite framework, monitoring compliance with limits, and overseeing risk policy implementation. The Asset Liability Committee, chaired by the Chief Financial Officer, manages capital, funding, liquidity, investment, market risk, and asset/liability activities in compliance with policies and regulations. The company follows a “three lines of defense” approach: the first line includes the Chief Executive Officer, business unit presidents, and Chief Financial Officer who initiate risk-taking; the second line includes the Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Operational Risk Officer, and control groups who oversee risk-taking; the third line is the Internal Audit Group, which provides independent assessments of the first and second lines. Credit risk is defined as loss due to default or changes in credit quality and is divided into individual and institutional categories. Individual credit risk arises from consumer and small business charge cards, credit cards, and term loans, involving millions of customers across geographies and industries, with risk generally correlated to economic trends like unemployment and GDP growth. Business unit leaders and Chief Credit Officers manage this risk, guided by the Individual Credit Risk Committee (ICRC), which ensures compliance with ERMC guidelines and escalates issues as needed. Sophisticated proprietary scoring and decision-making models using spending, payment history, and credit bureau data support credit risk management. Institutional credit risk arises in CS, ICS, GMNS, investment, and liquidity activities, characterized by lower loss frequency but higher severity, influenced by both economic conditions and client-specific events. Business units are supported by Chief Credit Officers guided by the Institutional Risk Management Committee (IRMC), which implements the Institutional Credit Risk Management Policy, makes investment decisions, ensures underwriting standards, monitors exposures, and determines risk mitigation actions, formally reviews large exposures, and provides guidance to optimize risk-adjusted returns. A centralized risk rating unit assesses institutional obligors. The company has significant cobrand, rewards, merchant acceptance, and corporate payments arrangements with airlines, with Delta being the largest partner, including an exclusive cobrand credit card partnership and Membership Rewards redemption. The ERM program evaluates airline and travel industry risks, including cruise lines, travel agencies, and tour operators. Debt exposure is monitored for sovereign and non-sovereign customers and counterparties by geographic region and economic sector, with a focus on credit deterioration due to economic and fiscal weaknesses; as of December 31, 2022, gross credit exposures to high-risk countries were considered individually and collectively not material. Operational risk is defined as loss due to inadequate processes, people, systems, or external environment impacts, including regulatory non-compliance and third-party relationships. A comprehensive operational risk framework, approved by the ERMC, includes operational risk event capture, a project office for issue management, key risk indicators, and process and entity-level risk assessments. The Operational Risk Management Committee (ORMC), chaired by the Chief Operational Risk Officer, coordinates risk assessments and controls, oversees preventive and responsive efforts by Operational Excellence teams, and requires root cause analysis, impact assessment (operational, financial, brand, regulatory, legal), and resolution plans. Information and cyber security risk is defined as the risk of a security incident impacting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of customer, colleague, or proprietary information. The program uses advanced technology, a trained team, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, with controls for identification, protection, detection, response, and recovery. Information technology risk is the risk of events compromising processing, stability, capacity, performance, or resilience of IT systems, leading to financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts. The company manages IT risk through policies, procedures, governance, and controls to preserve system confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Privacy risk is the risk of financial loss, reputational damage, or legal action from violating laws, regulations, contractual obligations, or privacy policies in processing personal data. The Global Privacy Policy establishes data protection principles, and the Privacy Risk Management Committee, chaired by the Chief Privacy Officer and a sub-committee of the ORMC, provides oversight. Data management and governance risk is the risk of financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts from inadequate data governance or management practices affecting data accuracy, completeness, timeliness, comprehensiveness, or usability. The Enterprise Data Governance Policy defines in-scope critical data and lifecycle management requirements, approved by the ERMC. The Enterprise Data Committee, chaired by the Chief Data Officer and a sub-committee of the ERMC, provides governance and oversight. Third party risk is the risk from relationships with third parties or their subcontractors leading to unexpected outcomes or deviations. The Third Party Management Policy, approved by the Risk Committee and ERMC, sets procurement, risk management, and contracting frameworks, and the Third Party Lifecycle Management program guides identification, measurement, monitoring, and reporting of third-party risk throughout the relationship lifecycle. Conduct risk is the risk that colleagues fail to fulfill responsibilities in accordance with the Code of Conduct, policies, values, or laws, potentially increasing reputational risk. The Conduct Risk Management Policy, approved by the ERMC, requires annual risk assessments, preventive and detective controls, colleague training, and timely escalation of conduct issues, with consequence management for substantiated misconduct. The Conduct Risk Committee oversees conduct risk and escalates matters to the ERMC as appropriate. Compliance risk is the risk of legal or reputational harm, fines, penalties, or sanctions due to non-compliance with laws, regulations, internal policies, or ethical standards. The Global Compliance and Ethics organization manages compliance risk through assessment, control, monitoring, measuring, and reporting. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), chaired by the Chief Compliance Officer, identifies, evaluates, manages, and escalates compliance risks and has a dual reporting relationship to the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. The company has a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program that monitors suspicious activity and includes an independent risk assessment of its rules, with the Internal Audit Group reviewing processes for consistency.
